# Darśana of Kuṇḍalinī

## Opening

> पद्मोपविष्टां कुण्डलिनीं शुक्लवस्त्रां मनोहराम्
>
> — श्रीसरस्वतीस्तोत्रम् (रुद्रयामल)

I think that this description of सरस्वती deserves an adjective which I find hard to find.

कुण्डलिनी sitting upon a lotus, covered with what I perceive as holy and white, and what I witness, steals my heart.

Of course a number of adjectives stand in the source, but this line takes me somewhere totally different. I think there is a difference between Philosophy and दर्शन. Philosophy has more assertion than दर्शन. दर्शन is closer to landscape. Philosophy is closer to portrait.

## मन and माया

मन

माया

Notice how these two words start with the letter म. It has a similar sense as *me*, *my*, *mine*, मैं, मेरा, मेरी, and so on — as discussed in another post.

<!-- Narrative origin (parked): \sa{brahma} created \sa{manas}; it attained \sa{moksa} at once; \sa{visnu} assented; \sa{brahma} asked for a solution. Folk gloss parked with it: \sa{moksa} ~ मम् उच्च क्षयः -->

Without motion, मन does not hold. If it is not चंचल, it ceases. That is the problem माया answers.

## चंचल is not merely “fickle”

I need to put forward an argument: चंचल is not always *flickering*, *fickle*, or *spry*. Rather it implies “not stationary.” Whereas चंचल is an adjective, चंचलता becomes a noun. More often than not, चंचलता is taken quite lightly, and so synonymized with words like fickle, flickering, spry, and the like. My argument is that an ocean can be a bit more चंचल than usual — and there you go: tsunamis. Plural.

On the other hand, what does not being चंचल mean? Absolute rest — 0 Kelvin, if you like a picture. That is the cessation problem for मन.

Since मन is not चंचल, मन ceases to exist.

Solution? माया.

## The root of माया

The strict grammatical root: मा or माङ्.

If you open a strict Sanskrit dictionary or a Pāṇinian grammar text, the technical root (dhātu) for माया is मा or माङ्.

- **Root meaning:** मा means “to measure” (मापना), “to limit,” “to give shape,” or “to create/build.”
- **Suffix:** The feminine suffix -या (-yā) is added to this root to turn it into a noun.
- **Grammatical meaning:** मीयते अनया इति माया — “That by which something is measured or limited.”

Also let me bring another example of *ya*:

या: to go, to attain, or to move. (Note: the root here is the long vowel या, not just य.)

Example words: याति (*yāti* — he/she goes) or यात्रा (*yātrā* — journey).

## Measurement, धर्म, and why मन is चंचल

So मन is given a means to measure the extent of its existence. In a way, as soon as मन comes into existence, the set of tools मन has — termed as धर्म — includes माया: measurement whose धर्म includes differentiating between two unique entities in terms of value. You cannot apply a comparison operator between two alphabets, but between numbers you can — and that difference in value has significance. Difference may be favorable or unfavorable. Difference may exist between smaller and bigger intervals at the same time. माया acts as a tool to evaluate.

Hence माया is a reason मन is चंचल. Evaluation tends to impart lower value to stopping — hence to ceasing to exist. That offers a challenge against which the tools of मन act, resisting failure to uphold the existence of मन; hence मन is not let stop completely. It cannot be stationary. Hence मन is चंचल.

“मन has चंचलता” and “मन is चंचल” convey two different meanings, and the latter is preferable. It is not something मन *has*; it is something मन *is*.

## What is चंचलता for मन?

What is चंचलता when we are talking about मन?

What is मन? Answer: मन is चंचल.

Where is मन? Inside this body.

Who is मन? I am.

I am चंचल. I have a set of factors acting as tools to resist failure to uphold the extent of my existence. One of these factors is माया. Another is perception used to measure (perhaps a subset of माया — a measuring perspective).

Look around. My claim is that there does not exist any form of life which does not measure or evaluate.

Just as माया keeps मन not stationary — hence existent — the mechanism of evaluation cannot be functional without perception and perspective.

With perception and perspective, evaluation renders a value to a scenario, either evident or estimated, differentiates between other scenarios, and hence introduces drive and bias based on the value difference.

The dimensions of this valuation system are what tradition calls the षड्रिपु — the six:

काम
क्रोध
लोभ
मद
मोह
मात्सर्य

### The gate — coin

Think about it like the following. The perception from perspective delivers a landscape which gets evaluated. There is a gate, and evaluation always rattles the gate. A system is set up which sends a coin. Whenever the gate rattles — whether you attempted for it or not — the gate sends a coin. This coin, when you receive it, the evaluation renders drive towards the coin. With respect to the gate, the possibility of challenge and the strength in the challenge diminish as long as the coins are received. Gate never gets opened; you get dopamine release; everyone is happy.

If somehow you decide no — I am going to open the gate — you have to fight against the coins you valued so much. If you manage to open the gate despite a surge of coins, you pass through it; henceforth you can probably say that the gate is the gate of काम.

Similarly, there are six gates, at least — one for each of the षड्रिपु. They are not a ladder. They need not open in sequence; more than one can rattle at once.

### The gate — Indra’s sabhā

The same pattern is like Indra’s sabhā. When a sādhu’s tapas grows strong enough that the order is threatened, the sabhā rattles. Indra does not debate the sādhu into stopping; he sends an apsarā — enjoyment, beauty, distraction — so that the sādhu enjoys life and the ascent breaks. Sabhā quiet again.

So with the gate: rattle, envoy of enjoyment (the coin), drive toward that envoy, challenge weakened, gate closed. Refuse the surge and pass, and you have named which षड्रिपु-gate it was.

### What मन cannot do — and what these gates are

What मन is not capable of by default is control of the gates. It undergoes the rattle and the coin; it does not own the dispatch. That is why माया can keep मन from मोक्ष: the stay-alive valuation structure runs whether “I” planned it or not.

In this दर्शन, these gates *are* the कुण्डलिनीs. Not a portrait of a single serpent only — the coiled locks of valuation that keep the landscape from resting. Some say such locks sit in the spine; that is one reason the word carries *kuṇḍala*, the coil. I am not settling anatomy here. I am settling what I see: six coils of the षड्रिपु, Indra-sabhā in the body of evaluation.

माया keeps मन from मोक्ष. So when the gates are open — not as a sequence of levels, but as the release of this whole enable-structure — मोक्ष occurs. The fiercest coin, when the whole structure is at risk, I think is pure panic.

That is my दर्शन of कुण्डलिनी: not an absent object behind the videos, but these gates — the ones that rattle, pay, and try to keep the lotus-seated, white-clad, heart-stealing presence from being passed through. The adjective I still cannot find may simply be that she is seen this way.
